title: Responsibility for 1914 is still argued
body: Annika Mombauer's 2015 survey in Central European History treats the origins of the First World War as an open argument, not a closed verdict. She recounts Fritz Fischer's intervention in the 1960s: Fischer argued that decision-makers in Berlin deliberately unleashed a war. A later consensus, as she describes it, gave Germany a larger share of responsibility than the other great powers without everyone accepting a fully premeditated plan, and it also found that leaders in Vienna welcomed a war on Serbia. Christopher Clark's 2012 book The Sleepwalkers, she writes, rejects the search for a single guilty party, is more critical of Serbia and the Entente, and is more lenient toward Germany and Austria-Hungary. The book split historians. This card does not choose Fischer's account or Clark's. It records that qualified historians, using overlapping archives, still weight the July 1914 decisions differently.

sources.title: Guilt or Responsibility? The Hundred-Year Debate on the Origins of World War I
sources.author: Annika Mombauer

said_by: Annika Mombauer's survey of the historiography, Central European History, 2015

contested_views.position: Berlin's decision-makers deliberately unleashed war, and Germany bears the main share of responsibility.
contested_views.held_by: Fritz Fischer in the 1960s, as summarized by Mombauer

contested_views.position: The crisis was a shared failure across capitals; searching for one guilty state misdescribes it. Serbia and the Entente deserve more critical weight.
contested_views.held_by: Christopher Clark, The Sleepwalkers, as summarized by Mombauer
